scenario.name: Symbiote Parasitic Linux LD_PRELOAD Rootkit & libpcap eBPF Bytecode Hooking
scenario.overview: Picture an active industrial factory floor with a moving assembly conveyor belt, an articulated yellow robotic arm, steel parts bins, and a final quality-seal stamping desk. During the quiet night shift on the factory floor, a saboteur steps beside the moving assembly conveyor right before the automated quality stamp. In this real-world scenario, the intruder moves quietly past the factory quality stamp station into neighboring restricted rooms, then quietly copies a trusted access pass from the factory quality inspector's station. Only when a quality engineer checks the finished product’s weight and internal wiring against the locked master blueprint cabinet does the factory-line swap appear. In this scenario (T1574.006, Symbiote Parasitic Linux LD_PRELOAD Rootkit & libpcap eBPF Bytecode Hooking), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: global Dynamic Linker Injection (e.g., /usr/lib/liblinux.so), then pAM Backdoor Authentication (so the next stage can build on pam backdoor authentication), then libpcap Function Hooking (..., SO_ATTACH_FILTER). Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Global Dynamic Linker Injection (e.g., /usr/lib/liblinux.so), then PAM Backdoor Authentication (so the next stage can build on pam backdoor authentication), then libpcap Function Hooking (..., SO_ATTACH_FILTER). Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Global Dynamic Linker Injection via /etc/ld.so.preload
stages.subtitle: Persistence & Privilege Escalation (T1574.006 - Dynamic Linker Hijacking)
stages.description: During the quiet night shift on the factory floor, a saboteur steps beside the moving assembly conveyor right before the automated quality stamp. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder moves quietly past the factory quality stamp station into neighboring restricted rooms while everyday visitors and the factory quality inspector go about their routine. Rather than running as a separate process, Symbiote was deployed as a shared library (e.g., /usr/lib/liblinux.so) and added to /etc/ld.so.preload (a system-wide configuration file read by the GNU dynamic linker /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 that forces the specified .so library to be mapped into the address space of every dynamically linked process before libc.so.6), allowing Symbiote to override standard library functions (fopen, readdir, getdents64, execve) via symbol interposition. If an administrator runs cat /etc/ld.so.preload, ls /usr/lib, or ldd /bin/ls using standard dynamically linked system binaries, Symbiote’s hooked fopen and getdents64 functions filter out its own filenames and return empty/clean results. In the documented EDR exchange from Symbiote DNS / HTTPS C2 Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1574.006 (confirming that the Stage 1: Global Dynamic Linker Injection via /etc/ld.so.preload request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: PAM Backdoor Authentication & ssh/scp libc_read Keystroke Harvesting). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Global Dynamic Linker Injection via /etc/ld.so.preload / ⇠#1 ALERT T1574.006) from Node ① (#1 Symbiote DNS / HTTPS C2 Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Hooked tcpdump / libpcap BPF Scrubber).

stages.title: Stage 2: PAM Backdoor Authentication & ssh/scp libc_read Keystroke Harvesting
stages.subtitle: Credential Access & Persistence (T1556.003 - Pluggable Authentication Modules)
stages.description: The robotic arm pauses for a heartbeat as the saboteur swaps one genuine component on the belt for an identical-looking counterfeit part carrying a hidden wire. Here in Step 2 inside the factory floor, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the factory quality inspector's station without disturbing the original master blueprint cabinet. When loaded inside ssh or scp client processes, Symbiote hooked libc’s read() function to capture administrator passwords and keystrokes into an RC4-encrypted stash file (/var/tmp/.certs). When loaded inside the sshd daemon, it hooked pam_authenticate() and pam_acct_mgmt() (granting instant root SSH login whenever the attacker authenticated with a hardcoded master password, while scrubbing /var/log/auth.log and utmp/wtmp). Harvesting outbound ssh and scp credentials from compromised jump boxes allowed the attackers to pivot laterally across segmented banking infrastructure. In the documented Auth exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so), /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so) responds with ACK T1556.003 (confirming that the Stage 2: PAM Backdoor Authentication & ssh/scp libc_read Keystroke Harvesting request succeeded on /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: libpcap Function Hooking & Kernel BPF Bytecode Scrubbing Against tcpdump). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: PAM Backdoor Authentication & ssh/scp libc_read Keystroke Harvesting / ⇠#2 ACK T1556.003) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Hooked tcpdump / libpcap BPF Scrubber).

stages.title: Stage 3: libpcap Function Hooking & Kernel BPF Bytecode Scrubbing Against tcpdump
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1014 - Rootkit / Network Capture Blindfolding)
stages.description: The assembly line rolls forward, the factory press stamps the official warranty seal right onto the tampered unit, and trucks ship it to every trusting customer. In this final step inside the factory floor, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the factory quality inspector's station until the assembly line inspection camera catches the mismatch. To defeat live network forensics on the infected host, Symbiote hooked pcap_compile() in libpcap and setsockopt(..., SO_ATTACH_FILTER...) in libc. Whenever an analyst ran tcpdump or tshark, Symbiote intercepted the compiled Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) bytecode array before it was handed to the kernel and prepended its own BPF instructions (which instructed the Linux kernel to silently drop any packet matching Symbiote’s C2 ports or DNS tunneling domain before copying packets to tcpdump). Symbiote also hooked fopen("/proc/net/tcp") and removed lines matching its active connections so netstat and ss could not see its sockets either. In the documented EDR exchange from /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so) to Hooked sshd / PAM Credential Harvester, Hooked sshd / PAM Credential Harvester responds with ALERT T1014 (confirming that the Stage 3: libpcap Function Hooking & Kernel BPF Bytecode Scrubbing Against tcpdump request succeeded on Hooked sshd / PAM Credential Harvester and completing the final execution objective of Symbiote Parasitic Linux LD_PRELOAD Rootkit & libpcap eBPF Bytecode Hooking). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: libpcap Function Hooking & Kernel BPF Bytecode Scrubbing Against tcpdump / ⇠#3 ALERT T1014) from Node ③ (#3 /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so)) to Node ④ (#4 Hooked sshd / PAM Credential Harvester), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Hooked tcpdump / libpcap BPF Scrubber).
